Well, hi, yeah, thanks for fitting me in. So, as for what brings me in... well, it’s been building up for a while, honestly. I’d say for the past year or so, I’ve just been having this issue where every little thing completely derails me. And I mean the absolute smallest things.

Or if somebody just walks past my office door. I had these glass walls put in a few years ago because I thought it was a great idea for company culture, you know, transparency and all that, but now it’s like every time an employee even walks by to get coffee, my brain just snaps right to them. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around me in the room. It’s in my own head, too. I’ll be right in the middle of looking at quarterly numbers or something important, and suddenly I have a totally random thought about my in-laws—like, wondering what my father-in-law is going to say about the upcoming holidays, or if they're visiting—and boom, it pulls me completely off what I’m doing before I can even stop it. Well, anxious? I wouldn’t really say anxious. It’s not like my heart is pounding or I’m sitting there worrying that the company is going to go under because I looked away for a second. Act on impulse without thinking about the consequences? Um... no, I wouldn't say that. I really don't think I do that. I mean, sure, I move fast. You have to move fast in business. But I wouldn't call it acting without thinking about what's going to happen next. Actually, it's kind of the opposite, because when you're the guy in charge, everything falls on your shoulders, right? I mean, I didn't even finish high school, so I don't have some fancy MBA or safety net to fall back on. Everything I built, I built by trusting my gut, but my gut is always calculating the risks. 

Like, people might see me make a quick call and think, "Oh, he's just being impulsive." For example, a couple of months ago, we had this supplier who kept missing delivery windows, and I just cut them off right in the middle of a phone call. Just said, "We're done, cancel the contract." My operations manager was absolutely freaking out, thinking I just ruined our supply chain on a whim. He was practically hyperventilating in my office, telling me I didn't think about the consequences. But I *did*. I already knew we had two backup vendors we could scale up, and I knew the late deliveries were costing us more in client goodwill than a temporary inventory dip would. I just processed all that in about ten seconds instead of calling a two-week committee meeting to debate it. 

So, no, I don't just do things recklessly. I might talk out of turn sometimes or jump into a project before the ink is completely dry on the proposal, but I always know what the stakes are. I'm not out here gambling the company payroll in Vegas or buying things we can't afford just for the thrill of it. I care way too much about my employees and the business to do something truly reckless like that. So, yeah, I definitely think things through... I just think them through a lot faster than other people expect me to, which I guess can look like an impulse to them, but to me, it's just being decisive. So no, I wouldn't say I ignore the consequences.

Organizing my time? Um, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble with that. I mean, I run a whole company, you know? You can't really do that if you don't know how to manage your time. I actually think I'm pretty good at it, all things considered.

I don't sit down and write out a meticulous to-do list every morning, color-coded by priority, because honestly, things change so fast in my line of work that a list like that would be obsolete by 10:00 AM anyway. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yeah, I mean, that really goes back to exactly what I was just telling you a few minutes ago. Focusing for a *long* time on just one single thing is... well, honestly, it's exhausting. It really is. 

Like I said before, I can start a planning document, or I'll sit down with one of my managers—take my VP of Sales, Mark, for example. Great guy, brilliant at his job, built our whole outbound strategy from scratch, but man, he loves to get into the granular details. So we'll sit down in my office, and for the first few minutes? I am completely locked in. I'm engaged, I'm tracking every metric he's giving me, we're going back and forth, and I'm totally in the zone. But if we stay on that exact same topic for too long... it's like a switch just flips in my head. 

I don't even mean to do it, it's not like I don't care about the sales numbers, but my brain just sort of unplugs and wanders off. I'll be sitting there looking right at him, nodding my head like I'm following along perfectly, and then I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I completely missed half of what was just said. I have no idea what he's been talking about for the last five minutes. It's incredibly frustrating, not to mention embarrassing, because then I have to stop him, swallow my pride, and say, "Hey, I'm really sorry, my mind went somewhere else—can you run that back for me?" And he has to start all over. 

And it's the exact same story with those planning documents I mentioned earlier. The first ten minutes, I'm a machine. I'm typing away, getting all the big ideas down. But asking me to sit there and focus on that one document for an hour or two without jumping to something else? It just doesn't happen. I have to break away, I have to open another tab, I have to check my email, because holding my attention on that one single track for a long stretch just feels almost physically impossible. It's like my brain just refuses to stay in one place for too long.

Controlling my emotions? Um, no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, you can't exactly run a successful company if you're flying off the handle every time something goes wrong, right? People look to you for stability. Like, just last week, we had this massive issue with our payroll software. The whole system just completely crashed on a Thursday, and Friday is payday. Now, a lot of guys in my position—especially guys who built everything from the ground up without a fancy degree or a trust fund, like I was telling you earlier—they might completely lose it. They might start yelling at the IT guys, kicking the trash can, just totally panicking. 

But me? I didn't do any of that. I just took a deep breath, walked out to the main floor, and told everyone that there was a glitch but nobody was going home without getting paid. Just laid it out plain and simple so people wouldn't worry. And then I just methodically sat down and worked with the bank and the software vendor for the next six hours straight until we fixed it. So, sure, I feel the stress. I feel the pressure, absolutely. It is like this heavy weight on my chest sometimes, especially when people's livelihoods are on the line and it all comes back to me. But I don't let it control me. I don't explode at my staff or break down or anything like that. 

I mean, sure, I might get a little animated when I am excited about a new deal, or I might talk a little louder than I need to when I am trying to make a point in a crowded room, but that is just passion, you know? That is just me caring about the work. It is definitely not losing control. And honestly, if I could not control my emotions, my assistant Sarah would have quit years ago. Waiting? No, not really. I mean, it's kind of funny you ask that, because I think a lot of people just assume that guys in my position—running a company, always moving, always onto the next big thing—would absolutely lose their minds if they had to just stand there and wait for something. But honestly, it doesn't bother me at all. I actually kind of... well, I don't want to say I enjoy it, but I definitely don't mind it. 

Take the airport, for example. I fly a lot for work, mostly domestic, visiting our regional hubs, pitching new clients, that sort of thing. And even with TSA PreCheck—which, let me tell you, is an absolute lifesaver if you travel as much as I do—sometimes you just hit a massive wall of people. Like, just last month, I was flying out of O'Hare on a Tuesday morning, and for whatever reason, the line was just wrapped all the way around the terminal. You look around, and there are all these guys in expensive suits huffing and puffing, checking their watches, tapping their feet, complaining to the staff. 

But me? I just see it as free time. It's rare downtime. I'll pull out my phone, I'll clear out my inbox, maybe shoot off a few quick texts to Sarah—my assistant, I mentioned her earlier, she's the one who keeps my life running—just to make sure the afternoon schedule is totally locked in. Or, if I don't feel like looking at a screen, I'll just stand there and run through the quarterly projections in my head. It's actually one of the few times during the day where nobody is actively knocking on my door demanding a decision right that second, you know? 

And it's the exact same thing with waiting my turn in a meeting or a conversation. If I'm listening to a vendor pitch or one of my department heads is giving a presentation, I can wait until they're completely finished to jump in. I mean, sure, I might have a dozen different thoughts and ideas firing off in my head all at once while they're talking, but I know how to hold off until it's actually my turn to speak. It's just basic professional respect, really. You can't run a successful boardroom if you're just talking over everyone the second a thought pops into your head. So yeah, waiting in line, waiting my turn... it's never really been an issue for me. I just use that time to get other things sorted out mentally.

Overly emotional on the inside? Um... no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, I know some people use that metaphor, right? The whole swan thing—gliding smooth and calm on top of the water, but underneath they're just paddling like crazy and completely freaking out. But that's honestly not me. 

I really think my exterior matches my interior. When you're running a company, you can't even afford to *feel* reactive, you know? It's not just about hiding it from the staff so they don't panic; it's about actually keeping your own head clear so you can make the right call. Like, take last quarter, for example. We had this massive supplier issue. A huge shipment of raw materials got held up at customs, completely out of nowhere. Now, a lot of guys in my position would be sweating bullets, lying awake at night, their stomach in knots, just feeling that internal panic and rage even if they managed to put on a brave face at the office. 

But me? I honestly didn't feel that spike of emotion. I didn't feel this overwhelming urge to scream that I had to suppress. I just looked at the logistics report—it was a Tuesday, I remember because Sarah had just brought in the revised weekly schedule—and I just immediately thought, "Okay, what is the workaround?" I didn't feel angry at the customs agents, I didn't feel devastated about the project timelines. I just instantly shifted into problem-solving mode. 

Because if you let yourself feel all those extreme emotions, even just internally, it clouds your judgment. It eats up your mental bandwidth. And my bandwidth is already maxed out with a hundred different decisions a day. I mean, sure, if someone cuts me off in traffic or something, I might get a quick flash of annoyance, like literally anyone would, but it doesn't linger. It doesn't consume me. I don't sit there stewing in it or feeling like my blood is boiling while I'm smiling through a meeting. I just process whatever the situation is and move on to the next thing. I really think that's why I've been able to scale the business the way I have, because I don't get bogged down in all those heavy, reactive feelings that seem to paralyze other people. I just... I don't really operate that way, inside or out.

I just dive right in. Sometimes I probably dive in a little too fast, honestly, before all the red tape is sorted out, but I just want to get moving. So, no, getting started is never the problem for me. I have more than enough motivation to go around.\n\nDoctor: Do you have trouble waiting for your turn or standing in line?\n\nPatient: Waiting? No, not really. I mean, it's kind of funny you ask that, because I think a lot of people just assume that guys in my position—running a company, always moving, always onto the next big thing—would absolutely lose their minds if they had to just stand there and wait for something. But honestly, it doesn't bother me at all. I actually kind of... well, I don't want to say I enjoy it, but I definitely don't mind it. \n\nTake the airport, for example. I fly a lot for work, mostly domestic, visiting our regional hubs, pitching new clients, that sort of thing. Like, just last month, I was flying out of O'Hare on a Tuesday morning, and for whatever reason, the line was just wrapped all the way around the terminal. You look around, and there are all these guys in expensive suits huffing and puffing, checking their watches, tapping their feet, complaining to the staff. \n\nBut me? I just see it as free time. It's rare downtime. I'll pull out my phone, I'll clear out my inbox, maybe shoot off a few quick texts to Sarah—my assistant, I mentioned her earlier, she's the one who keeps my life running—just to make sure the afternoon schedule is totally locked in. Or, if I don't feel like looking at a screen, I'll just stand there and run through the quarterly projections in my head. It's actually one of the few times during the day where nobody is actively knocking on my door demanding a decision right that second, you know? \n\nAnd it's the exact same thing with waiting my turn in a meeting or a conversation. If I'm listening to a vendor pitch or one of my department heads is giving a presentation, I can wait until they're completely finished to jump in. I mean, sure, I might have a dozen different thoughts and ideas firing off in my head all at once while they're talking, but I know how to hold off until it's actually my turn to speak. It's just basic professional respect, really. You can't run a successful boardroom if you're just talking over everyone the second a thought pops into your head. So yeah, waiting in line, waiting my turn... it's never really been an issue for me. We had this massive supplier issue. A huge shipment of raw materials got held up at customs, completely out of nowhere. Now, a lot of guys in my position would be sweating bullets, lying awake at night, their stomach in knots, just feeling that internal panic and rage even if they managed to put on a brave face at the office. \n\nBut me? I just instantly shifted into problem-solving mode. \n\nBecause if you let yourself feel all those extreme emotions, even just internally, it clouds your judgment. It eats up your mental bandwidth. I don't sit there stewing in it or feeling like my blood is boiling while I'm smiling through a meeting. I just process whatever the situation is and move on to the next thing. I really think that's why I've been able to scale the business the way I have, because I don't get bogged down in all those heavy, reactive feelings that seem to paralyze other people. I just... I don't really operate that way, inside or out.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to pay attention to details?\n\nPatient: Details? No. No, definitely not. Actually, it's kind of the exact opposite for me. I mean, you can't run an operation doing the kind of volume we do if you're letting the little things slip through the cracks. A lot of people think that guys at the top, the executives, just sit around looking at the \"big picture\" all day and leave all the granular stuff to the lower-level guys. But honestly? That is exactly how you go broke. Especially when you started from the bottom like I did. When you don't have that formal education to fall back on, you learn real quick that the devil is absolutely in the details. \n\nLike, just to give you an example, last Thursday we were in the final stages of renegotiating a massive lease agreement for our new warehouse space—the one I mentioned earlier that we're expanding into next month. If you don't manage the details, the details manage you, and I refuse to let that happen. So yeah, definitely not an issue for me. Restless? Yeah, you could definitely say that. Especially the quiet part. I just... I don't do "quiet" well at all. 

I mean, take meditation, right? Everybody in the business world is talking about mindfulness and all that now. I read this article a few months ago about how all these top executives meditate for twenty minutes every morning to center themselves before the day starts, so I figured, okay, I'll give it a shot. Claire was thrilled, she even downloaded this guided meditation app on my phone for me. So I sit down in the home office, close the door, close my eyes, and try to just... breathe. Man, I think I lasted maybe ninety seconds. The silence was just deafening. It actually felt physically uncomfortable. I couldn't just sit there. 

And it's the exact same thing at night with Claire. After a long day, she loves to just decompress. She'll want to just sit on the couch in the living room, maybe have a glass of wine, no TV, no music, just quiet time together to unwind. Which sounds great in theory, it really does. I want to be that guy who can just sit and enjoy a peaceful moment with his wife. But after about two or three minutes of just sitting there in the dead quiet, it literally gets under my skin. It's like this crawling sensation, this tension that just builds up in my chest and my arms, and I feel like I absolutely have to *do* something. 

So I'll suddenly jump up and say, "Hey, I'm gonna go clear the rest of the dinner dishes," even though they're already rinsed and could totally wait until the morning. Or I'll pull my phone out of my pocket just to check the overnight shipping logs, or see if the West Coast regional manager emailed me back about a supply issue. And if I force myself to leave the phone alone and actually stay on the couch, I'll just start talking. I'll make these totally random comments about the dog shedding on the rug, or ask her if she thinks we need to power-wash the driveway this weekend, or bring up some random news headline I saw at lunch. Anything to just break the silence. 

Claire gets so annoyed. She'll look at me and say, "Can we please just sit here for five minutes without you buzzing around or checking your screen?" But I just can't. The quiet just gets so far under my skin that I can't physically tolerate it. I don't know how people just sit there and do nothing. It drives me absolutely crazy.

I just instantly shifted into problem-solving mode. \n\nBecause if you let yourself feel all those extreme emotions, even just internally, it clouds your judgment. It eats up your mental bandwidth. And my bandwidth is already maxed out with a hundred different decisions a day. I mean, sure, if someone cuts me off in traffic or something, I might get a quick flash of annoyance, like literally anyone would, but it doesn't linger. It doesn't consume me. I don't sit there stewing in it or feeling like my blood is boiling while I'm smiling through a meeting. I just process whatever the situation is and move on to the next thing. I really think that's why I've been able to scale the business the way I have, because I don't get bogged down in all those heavy, reactive feelings that seem to paralyze other people. I just... I don't really operate that way, inside or out.\n\nDoctor: Do you find it hard to pay attention to details?\n\nPatient: Details? No. No, definitely not. Yeah, exactly, like I was just mentioning a second ago, this definitely isn't a new thing at all. It didn't just start when I opened the business or anything. Looking back, this was absolutely around when I was a kid, too. 

I mean, I could probably dig up my old elementary school report cards if my mom still has them boxed up in her attic somewhere, and I guarantee you every single one of them would say the exact same thing in the little comments section at the bottom. It was always, "He disrupts the class," or "He's a distraction to the other students." Like I said, teachers were always, and I mean *always*, moving my seat. It was like a giant game of musical chairs but I was the only one playing. They'd put me next to the quiet kids hoping their good behavior would rub off on me, but instead, I'd just talk their ears off because I just talked way too much. I couldn't keep my mouth shut if a thought popped into my head. 

And the sitting still part... it was just impossible. I would just get up without asking, completely unprompted. The teacher would be right in the middle of a math lesson or reading a book to us, and I'd just stand up and wander over to the pencil sharpener, or go check out the class hamster cage or whatever, completely oblivious to the fact that you're supposed to sit there and raise your hand. 

And the blurting things out... man, it was just bad. Like I was saying about my fifth-grade teacher, they wouldn't even be able to finish asking the question. They'd get halfway through, like, "If Johnny has five apples and—" and I'm already yelling out "He needs more apples!" or just some random joke, completely stepping on their sentences before they could even finish getting the words out. 

So, yeah, to answer your question again, it's always been there. The distractions, the focus issues, the not being able to just sit and be a normal, quiet kid... it's just been my normal since day one. I've always been wired exactly like this.
